mcqs.question: According to Amdahl's Law, why can't adding unlimited cores yield unlimited speedup?
options: Because CPU manufacturers impose a hard cap on core count
Because a fixed serial fraction of the program can never be sped up regardless of core count, and it comes to dominate total time as the parallel portion's time shrinks toward zero
Because memory bandwidth is unrelated to core count in any real system
Because compilers cannot generate parallel code for more than 8 cores
mcqs.explanation: The serial fraction's execution time stays fixed no matter how many cores work on the parallel remainder, so as core count grows the serial part becomes the dominant, unshrinkable cost — capping speedup at 1/s. This isn't a manufacturer-imposed cap, memory bandwidth is a related but separate real-world factor, and there's no fundamental 8-core compiler limit.

mcqs.question: Why does synchronization overhead often get worse, not better, as more cores are added to a workload?
options: Because more cores automatically increase the clock speed of each individual core
Because more threads contending for the same locks or barriers means more waiting time, so contention on shared critical sections tends to increase with core count
Because synchronization primitives stop working correctly above 8 cores
Because adding cores always reduces the amount of serial code in a program
mcqs.explanation: More concurrent threads competing for the same shared lock or barrier increases contention and waiting time, which is exactly why synchronization overhead tends to grow with core count rather than shrink. Core count doesn't raise individual clock speed, synchronization primitives remain functionally correct at any core count, and adding cores doesn't reduce a program's inherent serial fraction.

mcqs.question: Why does the real-world speedup-vs-core-count curve typically fall below the theoretical Amdahl's Law curve?
options: Because Amdahl's Law already accounts for synchronization overhead and load imbalance
Because Amdahl's Law only models the serial-fraction ceiling; real workloads add further losses from synchronization overhead and load imbalance that the formula doesn't capture
Because real cores run at a lower clock speed than theoretical cores
Because Amdahl's Law overestimates the serial fraction of every program
mcqs.explanation: Amdahl's Law models only the effect of a fixed serial fraction assuming perfectly efficient parallel execution; it says nothing about lock contention or uneven work distribution, both of which further degrade real speedup below the theoretical curve. It doesn't already include those factors, isn't about clock speed differences, and doesn't systematically overestimate serial fraction.

mcqs.question: How does Gustafson's Law reframe the scalability question compared to Amdahl's Law?
options: It assumes a fixed problem size and asks how much faster it can be solved, exactly like Amdahl's Law
It scales the problem size with the number of cores, asking how much more work can be done in the same amount of time, rather than how much faster a fixed-size task finishes
It claims serial code doesn't exist in any real program
It only applies to single-core systems
mcqs.explanation: Gustafson's Law's key move is letting problem size grow with core count, asking how much larger a problem fits in a fixed time budget — the opposite framing from Amdahl's fixed-problem-size question. It doesn't deny serial code exists, and it's specifically a multicore/parallel-scaling law, not a single-core concept.
